title: Roll store-bought puff pastry to an even 1/8 inch with a spacer-ring rolling pin
instruction: Roll this puff pastry out to an even 1/8 inch (3.2 mm) thick.
context: Rolling dough out with a rolling pin, for a pie crust, cookies or pastry, is something most people have done at home. Store-bought puff pastry sheets (Pepperidge Farm's, the common US supermarket brand, 3/16 inch thick) are usually rolled thinner before use; the maker's own recipes roll a sheet to about 1/8 inch. Spacer rings that slip onto a rolling pin are sold by ordinary kitchen retailers for an even thickness. The rings set it only while both ride on the board, so the pin has to be kept level along its length: with one end lifted it leaves a wedge, thick on that side. Dough springs back, so it takes several passes. Uneven puff pastry bakes unevenly, rising higher and baking slower where it is thicker.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Full scale. An oiled maple board (mid brown, darker than the table) 30 cm deep (x) by 40 cm across (y) and 1.5 cm thick (a 12 x 16 inch board) lies fixed on the table, spanning x 10 to 40 and y -20 to 20, top at z 1.5, lightly floured. On it lies half of a thawed, still-cold Pepperidge Farm Puff Pastry Sheet (one sheet of the 17.3 oz box, about 24 x 23 cm and 3/16 inch thick, unfolded and cut in half): 11.5 cm (x) by 24 cm (y), 4.8 mm thick (132.5 mL, about 122 g), centered at x 24, y 0. Behind it a handled maple rolling pin (12 inch barrel, as the Frieling Classic with Handles: 53.3 cm overall, 0.73 kg) lies on its rings on the board with its axis along y at x 35, z 4.87: a barrel 6.1 cm across and 30.5 cm long (y -15.25 to 15.25), a blue silicone 1/8 inch spacer ring 6.74 cm across (3.2 mm proud of the barrel) and 1.5 cm wide on each end of the barrel (|y| 13.75 to 15.25, outside the pastry's sides), and dark wooden handles 2.5 cm across and 11.4 cm long (|y| 15.25 to 26.65), reaching past the board's sides without touching anything. The ring to board friction is 0.15 static, 0.10 dynamic: the real pin's barrel turns on bushings and rolls, while the sim's gripped pin slides on its rings, so its sliding friction is set low in place of rolling. The pastry is modeled: it has no collider, and is shown as 2 cm slabs as thick as the pastry there, colored by thickness (cream over 4.2 mm, golds down to golden at 2.9 to 3.5 mm on spec, tan and dark brown below 2.9 mm, which the model never reaches because the rings hold the barrel 3.2 mm up).
scoring: Thickness is read at fixed points, held 1 s at the end: the centers of the 2 cm squares of a grid lined up with the board's front edge and center line, wherever the pastry covers the point (about 96 points); each 2 cm band running along x is one row. The sheet is on spec when at least 90 % of the points are 3.2 mm (1/8 inch, the rings' gap) within 0.3 mm; 10 % allows for the outer row near the cut and rolled edges. It is even when the bands' average thicknesses are within 0.3 mm of each other, since a pin with one end lifted leaves a wedge that bakes lopsided. All the pastry must still be on the board. The pin is put away when it lies on its rings on the board or table, level within 3 degrees (rings within 5 mm of the surface), and let go (a release check: no gripper touching it), because a held or propped pin is not finished with. The trial scores 1.0 when the sheet is on spec, even and on the board and the pin is put away. It scores 0.5 when at least 90 % of the points are at most 3.7 mm but the sheet is not finished (about one pass left, or a slight wedge), or when the sheet is finished but the pin is not put away. It scores 0.25 when at least 90 % of the points are at most 4.2 mm and the sheet is even, one level pass from the 4.8 mm start. Otherwise it scores 0, including when the robot does nothing, makes a single stroke, leaves a wedge or pushes pastry off the board. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Where the arms end is not scored. There is no length rule. In the simulation only, the model presses the pastry while both grippers touch the pin. This is an approximation, because the sim's pin slides on its rings instead of turning and cannot tell rolling from pushing; a stroke with fewer hands presses nothing but is not penalized. The real trial has no hand rule: it scores only the measured sheet and the final pin state, so a sheet rolled partly or wholly with one hand scores like any other. Real trial: lay a 2 cm grid transparency on the sheet, lined up with the board's front edge and center line, and at the center of each square the pastry covers read the thickness with a digital tire tread depth gauge (zeroed on the board, foot resting on the pastry, pin pushed through): the same points the sim reads. A point under 2.9 mm, a hole, a tear or a spot where pastry stuck to the pin counts as off spec, since a ringed pin cannot press below 3.2 mm. Check the pin with a level app and a ruler, and the last frames for a finger on it.
reset_notes: The pastry is consumed: each real trial uses half of a Pepperidge Farm Puff Pastry Sheet, thawed as the box directs and still cold, unfolded on the floured board, its thickness checked with calipers, cut to 11.5 x 24 cm and rolled at once (chilled 10 to 15 minutes in the refrigerator first if it turns sticky, as the box says). Scrape the board clean and re-flour it, set the half sheet centered at x 24, y 0, lay the pin on its rings at x 35 with its axis along y, and check both rings are on the barrel ends.
fidelity: The pastry is a model (doughkit) with no collider: the pin rides on its rings, and each slice the barrel crosses is pressed to the gap plus half its excess (springback, an estimate), volume kept; it lengthens, not widens. It presses only while both hands touch the pin, since the pin slides rather than turns; the real trial has no hand rule. The dough gives no rolling resistance. It cannot tear or go below 3.2 mm; a depth gauge checks a real sheet.
